flavor: Spoon-shaped leaves with a sweet mustard snap and a lingering mineral finish — richer than bok choy, never bitter when grown in cold.
notes: Forms a low rosette that shrugs off frost and actually sweetens after cold nights. Harvest outer leaves or cut the whole head. Prime crop for unheated houses in winter.

flavor: Feathery leaves with a peppery, almost arugula brightness and a clean finish — the salad green chefs reach for when lettuce tastes like water.
notes: Cut-and-come-again. Bolts in long hot days, so spring sowings should be early. Fall crops are the most succulent. Excellent under cover.

flavor: Narrow strap leaves, milder than mizuna, with a juicy green-cabbage sweetness that stands up to soup and pickling.
notes: A Kyoto classic, less common in Western catalogs. Dense clumps; harvest like chives. More heat-tolerant than mizuna but still a cool-season star.

flavor: Glossy spinach-mustard hybrid flavor: sweet, spinachy, with a quiet mustard undertone. One of the most versatile cooking greens in Japan.
notes: Also called Japanese mustard spinach. 'Summerfest' holds quality in shoulder heat better than heirlooms. Stir-fry stems and leaves together.

flavor: Deeply blistered, dark leaves with a buttery texture and a mild, sweet brassica flavor — like tatsoi crossed with savoy cabbage.
notes: Exceptionally cold-hardy; a greenhouse winter staple. Slow to bolt. Beautiful in the bed and on the plate.

flavor: Lime-green ruffled leaves that eat like a tender lettuce with a hint of napa sweetness. The rare green that satisfies salad and stir-fry people.
notes: Fast and elegant. Baby leaves at 3 weeks, heads at 6. Prefers cool weather; greenhouse extends the fall crop deep into winter.

flavor: A cabbage–komatsuna cross: large, tender leaves with sweet cabbage depth and none of the sulfur bite of collards.
notes: Huge productivity. Cut leaves for months. More heat-tolerant than napa, more cold-tolerant than regular cabbage greens.

flavor: Purple flower stems with a sweet, asparagus-broccoli taste. The buds are the prize — delicate, nutty, and completely unlike heading brassicas.
notes: Grown for flowering shoots, not a leafy head. Cool weather intensifies the purple. Harvest stems with a few open flowers.

flavor: Tender stems and buds with a sweet, green-pea brassica flavor — the Cantonese standard for high-heat wok cooking.
notes: Fast. Harvest whole plants when buds form, before flowers fully open. Successions every two weeks in cool weather.

flavor: Thick succulent stems with a sweet, faintly bitter broccoli intensity. Oyster sauce exists for this vegetable.
notes: Needs more time than leafy choys. Fall plantings produce the thickest stems. Greenhouse keeps quality when nights drop.

flavor: A wrapped mustard head with serious heat that mellows to a round, pickled-cabbage richness when cooked. Essential for suan cai.
notes: Heading mustard. Cool nights keep it from turning fiercely hot. Direct sow; do not let it sit in heat or it bolts and toughens.

flavor: Burgundy-blushed leaves with a wasabi-like heat that cools into grape-mustard sweetness after frost.
notes: Ornamental and edible. Baby leaves for salad, large leaves for braising. Cold makes the color and flavor both more interesting.

flavor: Crisp, juicy midribs with a clean sweetness that kimchi was invented to celebrate. 'Bilko' heads are dense and resist bursting.
notes: Fall is the real season — spring crops often bolt in lengthening days. Needs consistent moisture. Clubroot-resistant strain.

flavor: Baby heads with celadon stems and a sweet, almost corn-like juice. More refined than full-size white-stem pak choi.
notes: Compact, uniform, and fast. Spring and fall. Heat makes it bolt; greenhouse in late fall is insurance.

flavor: Violet leaves over green stems; milder than red mustards, with a sweet pak-choi crunch and a faint berry-brassica aroma.
notes: Color deepens in cold. Best eaten young. A showpiece that actually tastes as good as it looks.

flavor: Aromatic greens with a resinous, herbal bitterness — like chrysanthemum tea crossed with spinach. The flavor of sukiyaki.
notes: Not a brassica. Cool weather keeps leaves tender. Harvest before buds, or let a few flower. Unique enough that people remember it.

flavor: Grown for the thick stem: crisp as jicama, with a mild lettuce-cucumber taste and a toasted-nut aftertaste when sliced thin.
notes: Leaves are edible young; the swollen stem is the point. Needs a long cool stretch. A Chinese banquet vegetable rarely grown in home gardens.

flavor: Long white roots that are juicy, mildly sweet, and only gently pungent — the daikon you grate over soba and pickle into takuan.
notes: Fall crop first. Spring sowings often go pithy or bolt. Loose soil is essential. Greens are a second vegetable.

flavor: Magenta-and-white flesh with a sweet, juicy bite and a tamed heat. Beautiful raw; keeps its color in quick pickles.
notes: A modern Korean-type winter radish. Best as a fall crop. Stores well. Sow later than summer radishes; it wants to size in cooling soil.

flavor: Pale green skin, shocking magenta heart. Sweet, crisp, and only mildly peppery — the radish that converts radish skeptics.
notes: Classic Chinese xin li mei type. Needs a long cool season to color fully. Spring crops can disappoint; plant for late fall harvest.

flavor: Jade flesh that is sweeter and juicier than red radishes, with a fresh-apple quality and almost no bite.
notes: A northern Chinese keeping radish. Outstanding raw and in hot pot. Fall only in most climates.

flavor: A slender Kyoto turnip, white with a magenta shoulder. Tender, sweet, and the traditional pickle for senmaizuke.
notes: Harvest young. Fall crops are sweeter. The greens are as good as the roots. Rare outside Japanese seed lists.

flavor: Flat leaves with a true garlic perfume and a green-onion juiciness. The flavor of dumplings, jiaozi, and Korean buchimgae.
notes: Perennial once established. Start from seed in spring or divide. Yellow (blanched) nira is a delicacy. Flowers are edible.

flavor: A wild, aromatic parsley-celery-chervil hybrid. Fresh, slightly bitter, and unmistakably Japanese in soups and chawanmushi.
notes: Woodland plant: part shade, steady moisture. Can overwinter in mild climates and unheated houses. Treat as a perennial in shade.

flavor: Cinnamon, basil, mint, and cumin in one ruffled leaf. The herb that makes sashimi, umeboshi, and summer noodles taste like themselves.
notes: Tender. Needs warmth to germinate — soak seed. Pinch for bushiness. Self-sows once happy. Greenhouse gets you an earlier, longer season.

flavor: Dark purple leaves with the same spice-basil perfume as green shiso, plus a berry-ink tannin used to color umeboshi.
notes: Same warmth needs as green shiso. Stunning in the garden. Red is the pickling leaf; green is the fresh herb. Grow both.

flavor: Long scarlet shanks with a sweet, round onion flavor and none of the harshness of storage onions. Stunning sliced raw.
notes: Japanese negi type. Can be blanched for longer white/red stems. Hardy. Sow spring or late summer for overwintering in mild areas.

flavor: A fat, leek-like Japanese onion with a melting sweetness when braised. Famous from Shimonita, Gunma — one of Japan’s great vegetables.
notes: Needs a long season and hilling. Fall transplant or early spring. Worth the wait. Greenhouse or cloche speeds the start.

flavor: Red-orange kabocha with dry, chestnut-sweet flesh. Denser and more candied than butternut, with a roasted-squash perfume.
notes: Short-vine, earlier than many maximas. Needs heat and frost-free ripening. Greenhouse or black plastic helps cool climates.

flavor: Teardrop squash with dry, nutty, almost chestnut flesh and edible skin. The French potimarron — a flavor benchmark for winter squash.
notes: Stores for months. Plant after soil is truly warm. One of the few squash worth growing instead of buying.

flavor: Thin-walled Italian frying pepper that ripens to candy-sweet, fruity, and almost jammy. Slow Food’s Ark of Taste for a reason.
notes: Not a hot pepper. Transplant after nights stay above 10°C. Greenhouse weeks matter in short seasons. Dry or fry when fully red.

flavor: Blistered, salted, and eaten whole: thin skin, green-pepper sweetness, and the occasional hot one. The best bar snack that is a vegetable.
notes: Harvest small and green. Productive in heat. Greenhouse gives an earlier first pick. One in ten fruits runs hot — that is the game.

flavor: Galician frying pepper: grassy, sweet, and mostly mild, with the same roulette heat as shishito but a deeper, oil-friendly flesh.
notes: Pick at 4–5 cm. Larger fruits run hotter. Loves heat; unheated greenhouse is a real advantage in maritime climates.

flavor: Husked golden berries that taste like pineapple, vanilla, and cherry tomato. A fruit people eat standing in the garden.
notes: Drop when ripe — that’s the harvest cue. Self-sows. Needs a warm start; greenhouse transplanting pays off. Polish heirloom.

flavor: A climbing moschata eaten young like zucchini — nutty, never watery, with a seed cavity in the bell so the neck is all flesh.
notes: Resistant to many squash borers (vines). Harvest at 30 cm for summer use, or let mature as a keeping squash. Needs a trellis.

flavor: Ribbed Chinese cucumber: crisp, mild, and never bitter, with thin skin you do not peel. The slicing cucumber of northern China.
notes: Grows 30–40 cm. Trellis for straight fruit. More heat-tolerant than European types. Greenhouse cucumbers start earlier and cleaner.

flavor: Thumbnail watermelons that pop with lime-cucumber juice. A pickle and snack crop people grow once and then never skip.
notes: Long season; start indoors. Tiny fruit, huge vines. Greenhouse or a warm wall helps north of zone 7.

flavor: Leaf broccoli from southern Italy: sweet, mineral, and more interesting than calabrese, with tender stems like rapini without the bitterness.
notes: Grown for leaves and shoots, not a big head. Cool-season. Cut-and-come-again. A chef green that is still uncommon in home beds.

flavor: Classic Pugliese rapini: bitter-sweet shoots and buds with a mustard edge that olive oil and garlic were made to tame.
notes: Quarantina is a 40-day type. Spring and fall. Heat makes it bolt to flowers — still edible, just smaller. Fall is kinder.

flavor: Artichoke’s wild cousin, grown for blanched leaf stalks: bittersweet, nutty, and deeply Mediterranean. A slow luxury vegetable.
notes: Long season. Blanch stalks 3–4 weeks before harvest. Perennial in mild winters. Start early indoors or in a greenhouse.

flavor: Tiny berries that taste like wild woodland strawberries — intense perfume, rose, and honey. Flavor density supermarket berries forgot.
notes: Day-neutral, no runners. Sow early; needs light to germinate. Fruit the first year from an early start. Shade in hot summers.

flavor: Cilantro’s heat-proof cousin: lemon, cilantro, and a peppery tickle. The herb of gỏi gà and many southern Vietnamese tables.
notes: Tender perennial. Start in warmth; it hates cold soil. Greenhouse or a bright windowsill through winter. Usually grown from cuttings, seed is slow.

flavor: Anise-clove basil that holds in a hot wok. Sweeter and more perfume-heavy than Genovese, with purple stems that mark a proper phở plate.
notes: Transplant into real heat. Pinch flowers for leaf. Greenhouse basil is earlier and more abundant. 'Siam Queen' is an All-America winner for a reason.

flavor: Sawtooth leaves with a louder, longer cilantro flavor that does not vanish in soup. Central to sofrito, larb, and many Vietnamese broths.
notes: Likes heat, moisture, and a little shade. Bolts in long days; greenhouse or shade cloth helps. Perennial in frost-free climates.

flavor: Leaves and flowers taste like licorice-mint tea. A North American native that makes fruit, salads, and cold drinks more interesting.
notes: Hardy perennial. Sow spring. Bees wreck the flowers in the best way. Drought-tolerant once established.

flavor: Young leaves taste exactly like cucumber water — cooling, green, and clean. A medieval salad herb that still earns a bed.
notes: Evergreen in mild winters. Clip often to keep leaves tender. Direct sow early. Unheated greenhouse keeps a winter picking patch.

flavor: Celery turned up to eleven: leaf, stem, and seed all carry a deep, savory, Maggi-like intensity. A little goes a long way in broth.
notes: Huge hardy perennial. Sow cold or stratify. Plant once. One plant is enough for a household.

flavor: Resinous, medicinal, and a little wild — the herb that makes black beans taste Mexican. Not a background note; a signature.
notes: Heat lover. Self-sows aggressively in warm climates. Transplant after frost. Greenhouse start for short seasons.

flavor: Succulent, mild, and slightly sweet discs — the winter salad green that does not sulk in cold the way lettuce does.
notes: Native to western North America. Peak in cool, wet weather. Self-sows. A greenhouse winter crop par excellence.

flavor: Nutty, buttery rosettes. The French winter salad that makes greenhouse lettuce look like a compromise.
notes: Germinates in cool soil; heat is the enemy. Direct sow. 'Vit' is a large-seeded Dutch type. Unheated greenhouse is ideal.

flavor: Andean tubers with a lemon-bright, slightly acidic crunch that mellows to squash-like sweetness after sun-curing.
notes: Forms tubers only as days shorten — a late-fall harvest. Plant after frost. Needs a long season; greenhouse or cloche in autumn helps tubers size.

flavor: Crisp, juicy storage roots that taste like pear, apple, and jicama. Eaten raw. A dessert vegetable from the Andes.
notes: Needs a long warm season. Plant tubers after frost. Dig after foliage dies back. Greenhouse or a sheltered site in cool climates.

flavor: Beefsteak that ripens green-amber with a spicy, sweet, almost tropical flesh. One of the loudest-flavored heirlooms, not just a novelty color.
notes: Indeterminate, large fruit. Needs heat and a long season. Greenhouse or high tunnel changes everything in cool summers.

flavor: Variegated Chesapeake heirloom with clean heat and a bright, seafood-friendly pepper flavor. Historically used in crab and fish houses.
notes: Striking white-and-green foliage. Heat like a cayenne, fruit smaller. Transplant after frost. Greenhouse for a head start.

flavor: A mustard green that hits the sinuses like real wasabi — green, volatile heat that fades to sweetness. Not arugula, despite the nickname.
notes: Baby leaf in 21 days. Full size for braising. Cool weather keeps the heat pleasant instead of harsh. Fast greenhouse crop.

flavor: Young fenugreek greens: maple-bitter, celery-fresh, and the backbone of aloo methi. The dried leaf is kasuri; this is the garden version, loud and green.
notes: Cut-and-come-again in cool weather. Direct sow thickly; eat thinnings. Heat makes it tough and seedy. Fall and an unheated house are kinder than late spring.

flavor: The mustard of sarson da saag: broad, succulent leaves with a round heat that cooks down to sweetness with makki and ghee. Not an ornamental purple mustard.
notes: Grown for greens, not seed. Spring and fall; frost sweetens it. Pair with bathua and spinach if you want a proper Punjabi mix. Greenhouse keeps a winter picking patch.

flavor: Holy basil with clove, pepper, and a medicinal sweetness Thai basil does not have. Purple Krishna is the intense one — tea, tadka, and the plant many households keep by the door.
notes: Tender perennial treated as an annual in frost climates. Transplant into real heat. Pinch for bushiness. Greenhouse or a sunny pot overwinters it indoors.

flavor: The leaf that makes South Indian tadka smell like itself: citrus, resin, and toasted allium. Dried curry powder is not a substitute.
notes: A frost-tender shrub. Seed is slow; most gardeners start a nursery plant. Keep in a pot and bring in before frost. Dwarf stays harvestable in a greenhouse or sunroom.

flavor: The classic Indian green chili: wrinkled, thin-walled, bright heat, and a fresh pepper snap. This is the chili in the crisper, not a cayenne for drying.
notes: Name means 'volcano.' Harvest green for everyday cooking; red for pickle and powder. Transplant after nights stay warm. Greenhouse weeks matter in cool summers.

flavor: Small clustered eggplants with thin skin and a creamy, barely bitter flesh — the size for bharwan, sabzi, and a quick baingan fry. Not a watery globe.
notes: IARI cluster type. Pick young and often. Needs heat; unheated greenhouse or black plastic helps maritime climates. Staking keeps fruit clean.

flavor: Classic Indian okra: long tender pods with a green-bean sweetness and only a little slime if you keep them small. The bhindi of bharwan and sukhi sabzi.
notes: IARI variety, productive in heat. Direct sow or transplant into truly warm soil. Pick every other day. Cool nights stall it; a greenhouse start is worth it north of the hot belt.

flavor: Bitter melon the Indian way: long, pointed, fiercely bitter, then nutty once salted or stuffed. The bitterness is the point, not a defect.
notes: Trellis the vines. Harvest young before seeds harden. Needs a long warm season; greenhouse or a south wall in cool climates. Soak seed. More bitter than the smooth Chinese type.

flavor: Bottle gourd with pale, mild, slightly sweet flesh that takes dal, kofta, and lauki halwa. A cooling summer squash, not a craft birdhouse.
notes: Pick tender at 20–30 cm; older fruit turns pithy. Climbing vine, so trellis. Warm soil. IARI ‘Pusa Naveen’ is a straight, early eating type.

flavor: Ridge gourd: angled, spongy-tender, and quietly sweet, with a cucumber-squash taste that loves jeera and tomato. Peel the ridges; keep the flesh.
notes: Eat young — fist-long, still flexible. Mature fruit is a luffa sponge, not dinner. Trellis. Heat lover; greenhouse gets fruit before cool nights.

flavor: The round Indian gourd: apple-sized, pale green, with a soft squash-cucumber flesh that is the sabzi of Punjabi summers. Nothing else in the catalog tastes like it.
notes: A true Indian crop, not a baby watermelon. Pick small and tender. Warm soil, full sun. IIHR ‘Arka Tinda’ is an early, uniform type. Short vines compared with lauki.

flavor: Chichinda / padwal: long pale fruits with a mild, slightly sweet squash flavor and a spongy bite that holds coconut and mustard-seed tadka.
notes: Hang a small weight on young fruit if you want them straight. Harvest at 40–60 cm, still tender. Long warm season; trellis high. Greenhouse helps the start.

flavor: Andhra’s sour leaf: lemon, sorrel, and a green tang that makes gongura pachadi and mutton the dishes they are. Small-leaf chitti is the sharper one.
notes: Roselle grown for leaves, not calyxes. Heat and sun. Cut often so it does not wood up. Tender; treat as a summer annual. A greenhouse start lengthens the sour-leaf season.

flavor: Red amaranth saag: earthy, mineral, and slightly sweet, with a spinach body that does not collapse into water. The summer green when palak has bolted.
notes: Cut-and-come-again. Loves heat that wrecks lettuce. Direct sow after frost. IARI red leaf type — stunning and edible. Greenhouse is optional; heat is not.

flavor: Malabar spinach: thick, mucilaginous leaves with a beet-green mineral taste. The poi saag of Bengal and the South — summer vine greens that laugh at heat.
notes: Not true spinach. Climbing; give a trellis. Transplant after frost. Red-stem type is the looker. Greenhouse or a warm wall in short seasons. Perennial in frost-free climates.

flavor: Hyacinth bean: flat purple pods with a rich, beany, slightly tannic bite that is the sem of undhiyu and many Gujarati and South Indian kitchens. Cook thoroughly; do not eat raw.
notes: Pole bean. Pick young pods; mature seeds need boiling. Heat lover, gorgeous in flower. Greenhouse start for northern summers. Never raw — lablab has toxins until cooked.

flavor: Yardlong bean, the bora of Bengal and barbati of the North: snap-bean crunch with a deeper, pea-like sweetness and burgundy pods that stay pretty in a stir-fry.
notes: Pick at 30–40 cm, before seeds bulge. Pole, so trellis. Loves monsoon heat. More productive in warmth than common green beans. Direct sow after soil is warm.

flavor: Jute mallow, the ewedu of Yoruba cooking and Egypt’s national green: mucilaginous, deep, and spinach-like with a toasted-okra richness. The soup thickens itself.
notes: Cut-and-come-again in heat. Direct sow or transplant after frost. Young leaves only. Cool nights stall it; a greenhouse start helps short summers. Also called krain-krain and saluyot.

flavor: Lagos spinach: tender celosia leaves with a mild beet-green mineral taste and no bitterness. The everyday pot herb of southern Nigeria, not the cockscomb in the flower bed.
notes: Loves heat that cooks lettuce. Direct sow after frost; cut often. Flowers are edible but leaves get smaller if you let it bloom. Greenhouse optional — warmth is the requirement.

flavor: Scarlet eggplant, the garden egg of West Africa and Ethiopia: small orange globes with a tomato-bitter snap when raw and a sweet, firm flesh when cooked. Not a watery globe eggplant.
notes: Also called mock tomato. Pick at orange, still slightly firm. Needs heat like eggplant. Unheated greenhouse or black plastic helps maritime climates. Striking on the plant.

flavor: The fluted pumpkin of Igbo kitchens: grown first for the leaves — rich, slightly bitter, and meaty — and later for huge, oil-seeded fruit. This is ugu soup, not pie pumpkin.
notes: Long, hungry vine. Needs a long warm season; greenhouse or a south wall in cool climates. Soak seed. Harvest shoots and leaves continuously; fruit is a bonus in hot summers.

flavor: Grown for the fat, nutty white seeds that thicken egusi soup — toasted, almost pistachio-pumpkin. The fruit flesh is bland; the seed is the crop.
notes: A true West African melon, not a picnic watermelon. Long warm season. Dry and roast seeds. Greenhouse or black plastic helps the start. Give it room to sprawl.

flavor: African horned cucumber: jelly flesh that tastes like banana, lime, and cucumber in one spoon. The fruit people cut as a showpiece and then actually finish.
notes: Kalahari native. Needs heat and a long season; greenhouse pays off. Harvest gold-orange with horns still firm. Treat like a cucumber vine on a trellis.

flavor: Burgundy pods and earthy, sweet beans — the niebe of West Africa, eaten as leaves (the first green) and as peas. Deeper than a supermarket black-eyed pea.
notes: Heat and drought tough. Pick young pods, mature peas, or the tips as greens. Direct sow into warm soil. A true dual-purpose African staple, not just a cover crop.

flavor: Gomenzer in a heat-proof suit: kale-mustard leaves with a clean, cabbage-sweet bite and none of the sulfur funk of tired collards. Ethiopia’s brassica, selected in Texas for greens.
notes: More heat-tolerant than European kale, still sweet after frost. Spring, summer, and fall. Cut-and-come-again. Unheated greenhouse keeps a winter patch in mild climates.

flavor: East Africa’s weekly green: broad, sweet collard leaves that stay tender in soup with tomato and onion. The name means ‘to stretch the week’ — flavor that feeds.
notes: Hardy. Sow spring or late summer. Frost sweetens it. Slow-pick the lower leaves. Unheated greenhouse or a mild winter keeps it producing when lettuce has quit.

flavor: Spider plant, the African cabbage of the Sahel and East Africa: mustard-bright leaves with a peppery, slightly bitter snap that mellows in a tomato stew.
notes: Indigenous African green, not ornamental cleome. Heat lover. Direct sow after frost; harvest young shoots. Self-sows once happy. Fast summer saag when brassicas have bolted.

flavor: Mnavu / managu: tender nightshade greens with a deep, spinach-bitter richness that milk or cream tames. The everyday pot herb of Kenya and Uganda.
notes: Cultivated S. scabrum, not deadly nightshade. Cook the leaves; do not eat raw berries. Warm season. Transplant after frost. Cut-and-come-again. Greenhouse start for cool climates.

flavor: West African clove basil: pepper, clove, and thyme in one leaf. The scent leaf of pepper soup and jollof, louder and more medicinal than Thai or holy basil.
notes: Also called nchuanwu. Transplant into heat. Pinch for bushiness. Tender perennial — pot it and bring in before frost, or treat as an annual. Distinct from tulsi and Siam Queen.

flavor: African bird’s eye: small, clean, searing heat with a bright, almost citrus pepper flavor. The chili of piri-piri sauce, not a thick-walled habanero.
notes: Harvest red for sauce, green for a sharper bite. Compact plants, very productive in heat. Greenhouse weeks matter in cool summers. A little goes a long way.

flavor: Ridged North African / Middle Eastern okra: star-shaped in cross-section, meaty walls, and a deep green-bean sweetness. The ancestor crop, not a slimy afterthought.
notes: Okra is African in origin. Pick small. Needs truly warm soil — direct sow or transplant after nights stay hot. Distinct from Indian Pusa Sawani: shorter, deeply winged pods.

flavor: False roselle: maple-shaped maroon leaves that taste like cranberry, sorrel, and lemon. A sour salad and tea leaf from African hibiscus, not the gongura grown for stew.
notes: Tender shrub treated as an annual in frost climates. Transplant after heat arrives. Stunning hedge. Young leaves for salad; older for tea. Pot and overwinter indoors, or take cuttings.

flavor: Monk’s beard: saline, mineral, and snappy, like samphire crossed with young spinach. The Ligurian and Lazio spring green you eat with lemon and oil, not a background salad leaf.
notes: Sow in cool weather; heat makes it tough. Direct sow thickly. Harvest the succulent tips. A Slow Food curiosity that is still rare in home gardens. Greenhouse helps an early spring crop.

flavor: Roman chicory grown for the hollow, crunchy shoots: bitter, juicy, and the reason puntarelle alla romana with anchovy dressing exists. Not a leaf chicory in disguise.
notes: Fall and winter crop. Cut the inner shoots, soak in ice water to curl. Cool nights make it sweeter. Unheated greenhouse or a mild winter keeps it going. Direct sow or transplant.

flavor: The variegated radicchio that looks like a cream-and-wine rose: milder than Chioggia, with a nutty bitterness that takes olive oil and something sweet. A Veneto winter luxury.
notes: Needs a long cool finish to color. Sow for fall; spring crops stay greener and more bitter. Heads form as days shorten. Greenhouse or cloche helps in harsh winters. Don’t crowd.

flavor: Tuscan kale: blistered, blue-black leaves with a deep, almost nutty cabbage sweetness and none of the ruffly wateriness of supermarket curly kale. The green of ribollita.
notes: Hardy. Pick lower leaves through winter. Frost improves it. Sow spring or late summer. Unheated greenhouse keeps a picking patch when outdoor growth stalls.

flavor: The fractal Roman cauliflower: nuttier and sweeter than white cauliflower, with a precise, almost hazelnut crunch. A Lazio and Roman-campagna classic, not a novelty print.
notes: Cool-season and fussy about heat. Fall crops are more reliable. Transplant. Needs steady moisture and fertility. Greenhouse or shade cloth helps in warm spells.

flavor: Florence fennel: crisp anise-sweet bulbs that taste like licorice and celery had a well-dressed child. Shaved raw or braised, it is a proper secondo, not a garnish.
notes: Bolts in heat and long days — fall is kinder. Direct sow or transplant without disturbing roots. Hill the bulbs. Keep soil evenly moist. Greenhouse for an extra autumn crop.

flavor: Wild rocket: thinner leaves, longer heat, a peppery, nutty, almost sesame bitterness that supermarket salad rocket never reaches. The rucola of a Roman pizzeria.
notes: Perennial in mild winters. Cut-and-come-again. More heat-tolerant than annual rocket, still best in cool weather. Direct sow. Unheated greenhouse keeps a winter picking patch.

flavor: Ribbed Roman zucchini: dry, nutty flesh that does not water out in the pan, and male flowers worth stuffing. The zucchini people grow after they swear off watery supermarket fruit.
notes: Harvest small, with the flower on. Distinct from tromboncino (this is a bush/semi-vining pepo). Warm soil. Greenhouse start in cool summers. Pick every other day.

flavor: The warty sea pumpkin of the Venetian lagoon: dry, sweet, chestnut-dense flesh that gnocchi di zucca was invented for. A Slow Food squash, not a carving pumpkin.
notes: Long season. Needs heat and room to sprawl. Cure after harvest; flavor deepens in storage. Greenhouse or black plastic helps cool climates. Distinct from kabocha and red kuri.

flavor: Sicilian-style round eggplant, lavender and cream: creamy, almost seedless flesh with a mild, sweet flavor and none of the bitterness people blame on eggplant.
notes: Needs heat. Pick when glossy, before they harden. Unheated greenhouse or black plastic in maritime climates. The Italian cooking eggplant, not a long Asian type.

flavor: Bull’s horn pepper: long, curved, thick enough to roast, sweet enough to eat like fruit when red. The peperone of an Italian grill, distinct from skinny Jimmy Nardello.
notes: Sweet, not hot. Transplant after nights stay warm. Greenhouse weeks matter in short seasons. Harvest green for frying, red for roasting and conserving.

flavor: Fire-tongue beans: streaked cranberry pods with a rich, chestnut-beany flavor that pasta e fagioli and minestrone were built on. Fresh shelly or dried.
notes: Pole or semi-pole depending on strain. Pick plump for fresh shellies, or dry on the plant. Warm soil. More interesting than a generic kidney bean. Greenhouse start optional.

flavor: Lettuce-leaf Neapolitan basil: huge rumpled leaves, softer and sweeter than Genovese, with a perfume that holds in a caprese without turning minty. The basil of the South.
notes: Transplant into real heat. Pinch flowers. More heat-tolerant than tiny-leaf types. Greenhouse basil is earlier and cleaner. Distinct from Thai and tulsi already in the catalog.

flavor: Cucumber-bright leaves and flowers: the Ligurian herb of pansoti and ravioli di borragine, and a cool, honeyed edible flower. More kitchen than cottage garden.
notes: Hardy annual. Direct sow spring or fall. Self-sows. Young leaves for stuffing and soup; flowers for salad. Prefers cool weather. Unheated greenhouse for a winter picking of young leaves.

flavor: Vesuvian hanging tomato: thick skin, intense sweet-acid pulp, and a volcanic minerality. Stored in bunches through winter — the tomato of a Neapolitan pantry, not a beefsteak.
notes: Small pointed fruits with a nipple. Hang whole clusters in a cool dry room. Needs heat and a long season; greenhouse changes everything in cool summers. DOP of Vesuvius.
